question: A page builds its menu from `<div onclick="...">` elements. A reviewer asks for `<nav>` with real `<button>` and `<a>` elements. What is the main practical gain?
options: The CSS specificity of the menu becomes higher, so its styles can no longer be overridden
The browser downloads the page faster because semantic tags are shorter than `div` tags
Screen readers and keyboards understand them: focus, Enter and roles work without extra code
Search engines stop indexing the menu links, which keeps the crawl budget for content
explanation: Semantic elements carry meaning and built-in behaviour: a `<button>` is focusable, reacts to Enter and Space, and is announced as a button. A clickable `div` gives assistive technology nothing unless you rebuild all of that by hand.

question: How wide is this element on screen?
options: 250px
200px
240px
270px
explanation: With `border-box`, `width` includes padding and border, so the box is 200px wide and the content area shrinks to 150px. With the default `content-box` it would be 200 + 40 + 10 = 250px. Margin is outside the box in both cases.

question:
Given `
  • Home
`, what colour is the link?
options: Red, because a selector with an id outranks selectors made of classes
Blue, because the rule that comes last in the file always wins
Green, because two classes outrank one id plus one element
Black, because rules that conflict cancel each other out
explanation: Specificity compares ids first, then classes, then elements. `#menu a` has one id; the others have none, so no number of classes beats it. Source order only decides between rules of equal specificity.

question: You need a page layout with a header, a sidebar, a main area and a footer, aligned in both rows and columns. Separately, you need a row of buttons spaced evenly. Which tools fit?
options: Absolute positioning for both, with fixed pixel offsets
Flexbox for the page layout and Grid for the row of buttons
Floats for the page layout and tables for the row of buttons
Grid for the page layout and Flexbox for the row of buttons
explanation: Grid is two-dimensional: it controls rows and columns together, which suits whole-page layouts. Flexbox is one-dimensional: it distributes items along a single row or column, which suits toolbars and button groups.

question: Two scripts are in `<head>`: `app.js` depends on `lib.js`. You want them to download without blocking HTML parsing and still run in order. Which attribute do you put on both?
options: `async`: download one at a time, run before the parser starts on the body
`async`: download in parallel, run in document order after parsing ends
`defer`: download in parallel, run in document order after parsing ends
`defer`: download one at a time, run whenever each of them has arrived
explanation: Both attributes download without blocking the parser. `defer` scripts run in order once the document is parsed; `async` scripts run as soon as each one arrives, in any order, so `app.js` could run before `lib.js`.

question: A list has 2,000 rows and new rows are added while the page is open. Each row must react to clicks. What is the efficient way to wire this up?
options: One listener per row, added again for the whole list after every new row
One listener on the list that checks `event.target`, relying on event bubbling
An inline `onclick` attribute written into the HTML of every single row
A timer that checks every 100 ms which row is under the mouse pointer
explanation: Clicks bubble up from the row to its ancestors, so a single listener on the parent handles every row, including rows added later. This is event delegation: less memory, and no re-binding when the list changes.

question: This React component sends requests in an endless loop. Why?
options: The effect has no dependency array, so it runs after every render, and `setUser` triggers a render
The effect has no cleanup function, so React restarts it again whenever the fetch resolves
The `fetch` call is not awaited, so React repeats the request until a value is returned
The `user` state starts as `null`, so React keeps re-rendering until it becomes an object
explanation: Without a dependency array an effect runs after every render. The fetch sets state, state causes a render, and the effect runs again. Passing `[id]` makes it run on mount and only when `id` changes.

question: A React to-do list renders `items.map((item, i) => <Row key={i} ... />)`, and each row has its own text input. After deleting the first item, the text typed in row 1 appears next to a different task. Why?
options: Inputs inside a list are always reset by React whenever the list length changes
Keys must be strings, so React ignores numeric keys and creates every row again
Deleting an item mutates the array, and `map` then skips the first remaining row
Index keys shift after the delete, so React reuses each row's state for the wrong item
explanation: React matches old and new elements by key. With index keys, the item that moves into position 0 inherits the component state that belonged to the deleted row. A stable id from the data (`key={item.id}`) keeps state attached to the right item.

question: `count` is 0. After one click on this button, what does the component show?
options: 0, because React discards updates that are queued twice in a row
2, because each call runs immediately and sees the previous update
1, because both calls read the same `count` value from this render
An error, because state may be set only once in a single handler
explanation: Inside one render `count` is a constant (0), so both calls ask for 1. To build on the pending value, pass a function: `setCount((c) => c + 1)` twice gives 2.

question: A search box calls the API on every keystroke, so typing "javascript" sends ten requests. Which technique sends one request after the user stops typing?
options: Throttle: call the API on each keystroke but always cancel the first response
Debounce: restart a short timer on each keystroke and call the API when it finishes
Memoize: cache the result of each keystroke so the next one returns instantly
Polling: call the API every second whether or not the text has changed
explanation: Debouncing waits for a pause (for example 300 ms) before running. Throttling is different: it runs at most once per interval while events keep coming, which suits scroll and resize handlers.

question: A page has a purely decorative divider image and a product photo. How should the `alt` attributes be written?
options: `alt=""` on the divider, and a short description of the product on the photo
No `alt` attribute on the divider, and the file name of the photo on the photo
`alt="image"` on both of them, so that every image is announced the same way
A long keyword list on both of them, so that search engines rank the page higher
explanation: An empty `alt` tells screen readers to skip a decorative image. Leaving `alt` out makes many readers announce the file name instead. Informative images need a short description of what they show.

question: A React component starts a `setInterval` and must clear it later. Where should the interval id be kept so that storing it does not cause a re-render and the value survives between renders?
options: In `useMemo`, because it recalculates the id on each new render
In `useState`, because state is the only value kept between renders
In a plain `let` variable declared inside the component function
In `useRef`, because changing `ref.current` does not trigger a render
explanation: A ref is a mutable box that persists for the life of the component and is invisible to rendering. State would also persist but re-renders on every change, and a local `let` is recreated on each render, so the id would be lost.
